newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's Bhutto fears large-scale arrests.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's Bhutto fears large-scale arrests.

text.p: Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto said on Sunday she feared the country's caretaker government might carry out large-scale arrests of her party candidates before February 3 general elections

She also told British reporters after meeting British Prime Minister John Major she was not optimistic about a restoration of her government by the Supreme Court in view of the delay in the start of hearing of her challenge to her dismissal.
However, the Supreme Court on Sunday decided to begin hearing Bhutto's petition challenging her dismissal on Monday along with two other related petitions, the official APP news agency said.
Asked if her Pakistan People's Party (PPP) would take part in the elections, which Bhutto says will be rigged if President Farooq Leghari does not step down, she said:
"We will like to take part if there are no large-scale arrests of our candidates on the eve of the elections.

"We would most certainly like to take part. We had some reports that they (the government) might be planning to spoil our chances by going for large-scale arrests. That's why we are keeping our options open."
Leghari dissolved the National Assembly and dismissed Bhutto's three-year-old government on November 5 on accusations of corruption and misrule.

Bhutto, who denies the charges, has gone to the Supreme Court with a plea to restore the Assembly and her cabinet as it did after a similar dismissal of the government of her main rival, Pakistan Muslim League chief Nawaz Sharif in 1993, by then president Ghulam Ishaq Khan.

Asked about rumours of the possibility of her own arrest, Bhutto said: "There are so much rumours in Pakistan you never know what is true and what's not true. One of the rumours was that the Assembly would be restored and if that happened, they would like to arrest me beforehand so that I wouldn't be there to make a majority.

Asked if she was worried about the influence of the army in Pakistani politics, Bhutto said she felt the army, which has ruled Pakistan for about half of the period after the country's creation in 1947, had this time kept itself out of politics.
"There have been many, many sticky situations that had arisen.... And I think it is commendable that the army is trying to keep itself out of the picture.

But she accused Leghari of trying to drag the military into politics by forming last week a controversial Defence and National Security Council giving the chiefs of armed forces a formal advisory role in government affairs.

"I think it is a little sad that the president is trying to shore up his own sagging image by trying to form this new council. But I have found the army to show a remarkable restraint which as a teenager I would have never believed with our past history, and I commend them for that."
